No. 23· November 9, 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. The Trade Desk beats Q3 estimates by every measure and its shares still drop; Snap turns a profit the same week by leaning on subscriptions, because ad revenue alone grew just 4%. Scale is no longer enough on its own.

  2. Marks & Spencer apologizes within days after a Christmas post reads as a burning Palestinian flag; Target's new holiday campaign, its first under a new CEO, swaps "Hot Santa" for a comedy school instead, the opposite instinct in the same week.

  3. Clorox ships three AI-generated cat ads in 30 days at a tenth of the usual cost, right as Amazon opens its search results to outside stores and Instagram starts testing 90-minute videos to chase YouTube.

The world

The Trade Desk / exchange4media.com · November 9, 2026

The Trade Desk beats Q3 estimates and its own six-week Safari problem quietly closes, but the stock drops anyway

The Trade Desk reported Q3 2026 revenue of $739 million, up 18% year over year and above the $719.1 million Wall Street expected, with adjusted earnings per share of $0.45 against a $0.44 estimate and net profit up 16% to $116 million. Q4 guidance of at least $840 million also topped the $830.4 million consensus. The report lands with the Safari ad-serving block that had cut off adsrvr.org since September 14 (issues 15-22) now resolved in practice, iOS 27.2 having shipped publicly October 26, though neither Apple nor The Trade Desk has said so on the record. Despite the beat, the stock fell in after-hours trading.

Why it mattersA clean beat on every reported number still was not enough to move the stock up, which says more about how skeptical investors have gotten about ad tech's growth story than about this particular quarter.
247wallst.com, citing SEC filing · November 4, 2026

Snap turns profitable again, but only because costs barely moved, not because advertising did

Snap reported Q3 revenue of $1.72 billion, up 14% year over year but about 0.4% below the $1.73 billion estimate, with net income of $56 million against a $103.5 million loss a year ago; the swing came from total costs rising just 1% while revenue rose 14%, not from an advertising rebound. CEO Evan Spiegel said ad revenue growth "remains below our ambitions"; Sponsored Snaps revenue grew 56% and Snapchat+ and other paid subscriptions grew 84%, pushing paid subscribers past 30 million. The stock fell 10.6% in the hours after the filing. Q4 guidance sits at $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion.

Why it mattersSnap's profit this quarter came entirely from the subscription and cost-discipline side of the business, not advertising, the same split showing up across platforms this earnings season: the core ad business is the weak link, not the fix.
igeeksblog.com / dexerto.com · November 4, 2026

Instagram starts testing 90-minute videos, aiming straight at YouTube's podcast and long-form audience

Instagram began testing a new format called Features, horizontal videos up to 90 minutes long, with a small group of US creators including podcast host Emma Grede, beauty creator Monet McMichael and interviewer Preston Rakovsky, after earlier trials in Brazil. The tool lets creators link short Reels to a full-length video underneath, aimed specifically at podcasters and comedians who currently have to send their audience to YouTube for the complete episode. Instagram has not said when the format opens beyond this early group, but plans to expand it to tens of thousands of US creators.

Why it mattersInstagram spent years building its identity around short vertical video; testing 90-minute horizontal content is an admission that the real prize, podcast and talk-show audiences, lives in long-form, and short form alone cannot capture it.
ppc.land · November 4, 2026

Amazon opens its search results to outside stores for free, the same week a test finds bot-blockers stopping an AI shopping agent at 29 of 200 retailers

Amazon launched Shop Direct Merchant Workspace on November 4, letting retailers who do not sell on Amazon list their products in Amazon search results and in Alexa for Shopping at no cost, while keeping their own pricing, inventory, fulfillment and customer service; shoppers see a "Shop Direct" label and can click through to the merchant's own site or use Amazon's "Buy for Me" checkout. The same week, a separate test by Blend Commerce running an automated shopping agent against 200 US and UK retailers found 29, including Home Depot, Best Buy and Macy's, blocked the agent on two attempts, even though the same retailers' bot protection let ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude crawlers through.

Why it mattersRetailers are simultaneously being courted into agentic commerce by Amazon and unknowingly fighting it off with bot defenses tuned for the wrong threat, which is less a strategy than a sign nobody has decided yet what an AI shopper actually is.
Digiday Creator Strategies, New York · November 3-4, 2026

US creator ad spend is forecast to hit $43.9 billion in 2026, up 18.3%, as mid-tier creators grow ten times faster than macro names

Digiday's Creator Strategies event in New York, alongside its reporting, put 2026 US creator ad spend at $43.9 billion, up 18.3% from $37.1 billion in 2025, with the mid-tier creator segment growing roughly ten times faster over the past six months than macro-influencer deals, and showing a larger increase in sales and a slightly higher conversion rate. Only about 4% of all creators still earn more than $100,000 a year.

Why it mattersThe money is moving toward volume and conversion with mid-tier creators, not toward the handful of macro names brands used to chase first, a structural shift that keeps showing up every time this budget gets measured.

Campaigns & brand moves

marketing-interactive.com / newarab.com · November 1, 2026

Marks & Spencer apologizes after a Christmas post reads as a burning Palestinian flag

M&S shared an Instagram image from its Christmas clothing and home campaign on November 1, showing red, green and silver paper party hats burning in a fire grate, captioned "This Christmas, do what you love... like saying no to paper hats" under the tag #LoveThismasNotThatmas. The color combination read to many viewers as a burning Palestinian flag; M&S removed the post and apologized, saying the image had been shot in August as a purely festive visual with no political intent. Brand sentiment tracking shows both positive and negative coverage rising sharply after the post, from 18.3% positive and 12.9% negative beforehand to 24.7% positive and 20.6% negative after, a polarization spike rather than a clean swing either way.

Why it mattersNobody at M&S or its agency appears to have checked what three specific colors burning together would read as before publishing, the exact kind of unforced, checkable error that a single pre-launch look would have caught.
adweek.com / retaildive.com · early November 2026

Target ditches "Hot Santa" for a fictional gift-giving school in its first holiday campaign under a new CEO

Target's "Academy of Giftology" casts D'Arcy Carden, known for playing Janet in The Good Place, as the school's Chief Giftologist, in a nine-film holiday effort directed by Lucia Aniello, co-creator of Hacks, through production company Hungry Man. The campaign runs across broadcast, streaming, audio, out-of-home and social, and marks the first time Target has built creator content, interactive social formats and real-world activations directly into a holiday push rather than treating them as an add-on. It replaces the brand's recent "Hot Santa" character as the face of the season.

Why it mattersTarget is betting that comedy and a fictional premise travel better across platforms than a single mascot built around attraction, a lower-risk choice in a year when several rivals' holiday ads have backfired for the opposite reason.
contentgrip.com / marketingdive.com · rollout complete November 9, 2026

Clorox makes three AI-generated cat ads in 30 days at a tenth of the usual cost

Fresh Step, Clorox's cat litter brand, worked with AI-focused creative agency RECE (short for radical empathy and creative excellence) to go from brief to three finished 15-second spots featuring AI-generated talking cats in 30 days, at what the team describes as one-tenth the cost of a traditional production, with distribution on TV and social channels in place by November 9. RECE founder Toygar Bazarkaya described the process as closer to a tech startup's prototyping cycle than a traditional agency's.

Why it mattersWhen a mid-size CPG brand can get a finished, multi-spot campaign at a tenth of the cost and in a month instead of a quarter, the competitive floor for what "a real ad campaign" requires drops for everyone below it too, not just for Clorox.

Social trends

virlo.ai trend tracker · data as of October 29, 2026

The rock paper scissors food challenge is still early, built entirely around one plate and zero production value

  • Friends or family play rock paper scissors over a single large plate of food; the winner takes one huge bite while everyone else has to wait or run.
  • The format needs no script, no edit and no location beyond a kitchen table.
  • Largest version tracked so far: @itselainepark, at 9.2 million views (self-reported platform data, flagged as such).
  • Maturity: early, still room to grow as of this tracking date.
Why it mattersA format with zero production cost and a universally understood rule keeps outperforming anything that requires a concept pitch, the same lesson Clorox's AI ads are chasing from the production side.
virlo.ai trend tracker · data as of October 29, 2026

The paparazzi bowing trend has already passed its peak after racking up 528.7 million views

  • Creators film themselves in a mock paparazzi scrum, bowing and snapping photos of a friend walking past as if they were famous.
  • Total views: 528.7 million; single biggest video, from @presgmcknight, has 14.2 million (self-reported platform data, flagged as such).
  • Maturity: already past its busiest week heading into November.
Why it mattersA format can rack up over half a billion views and still be considered late by the time most brands notice it, the real argument for watching trend trackers weekly rather than catching up after a format peaks.
TikTok Creative Center · window October 27 - November 5, 2026

A mysterious "secret" original sound and a track called "Harrison" are TikTok's two fastest-growing audios right now

  • TikTok's own trending-sounds data shows two unlabeled original sounds, one tagged simply "secret" and one called "Harrison," as the platform's top-growing large audios.
  • The "Harrison" sound alone is attached to 434,600 videos; both are listed at peak stage.
  • Neither sound is tied to a celebrity, movie or song release, just a clip creators are building unrelated content around.
Why it mattersWhen an anonymous, unexplained sound outperforms music tied to real IP, it is a reminder that on TikTok the audio's familiarity to the algorithm matters more than its familiarity to a human listener.

What is working in content

adweek.com / mediapost.com

Comedy is replacing shock and sex appeal as the default tone for 2026 holiday retail ads

Target's "Academy of Giftology" (above) and Kohl's "The North Kohl's," which pairs returning "Kohl's Mom" Ellie Kemper with NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo in sketches about holiday gifting mishaps, both lead with broad comedy rather than the sexier, spectacle-driven holiday ads retailers leaned on in recent years. Both campaigns run across broadcast, streaming and social with an ensemble cast rather than a single breakout image.

Why it mattersIn the same season M&S got burned by a visual pun gone wrong, the retailers playing it safest are leaning on recognizable comedic performers instead of a striking single image, trading virality risk for something harder to misread.
contentgrip.com, on Fresh Step's RECE collaboration (above)

AI production cycles are compressing from a quarter to a month, and the cost is compressing with them

Fresh Step's three-spot campaign, brief to finished ad in 30 days at a tenth of the cost of a traditional production, is not an isolated case: it follows the pattern of agencies like Monks running AI agents unsupervised for 48-hour production sprints (issue 15) and points the same direction, production timelines collapsing from the quarter-long cycle brand campaigns used to require to something closer to a sprint.

Why it mattersOnce one mid-size brand proves a 30-day, one-tenth-cost campaign is possible and gets real distribution out of it, the old production timeline stops being the default and starts being a choice brands have to justify.

The historical bridge

Mount Rainier National Park, Washington, circa 1907

A photographer with a glass-plate camera and a tripod, shot specifically for a Kodak ad, shows what advertising imagery cost before stock photography existed

Around 1907, Eastman Kodak sent a photographer out along a dirt road in Mount Rainier National Park to shoot a man photographing the mountain for one of its advertisements, a single custom image requiring a trip, a tripod, a glass-plate camera and a dedicated shoot, exactly the kind of one-off production every advertiser needed before a cheaper option existed. In 1920, H. Armstrong Roberts founded one of the first true stock photography libraries in Philadelphia, publishing a catalog of ready-made images that small, local advertisers who could never afford a custom shoot could license instead; about half his early revenue came from advertising sales. The catalog model he invented, speculative images made once and licensed many times, became the industry's default for the rest of the century.

Why it still holds. Stock photography did not just save money, it lowered the floor of what counted as a professional-looking ad, letting advertisers who could never afford Kodak's kind of custom shoot compete visually with those who could. Fresh Step's AI-generated cats, built in 30 days at a tenth of a traditional production's cost, are doing the same thing to video a century later: not eliminating craft, but making a certain baseline of production value available to brands that previously had no way to afford it.
